problems.title: Counting FLOPs

parts.prompt: Time for n = 4096 at the GW-1's 1,536 GFLOP/s, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) $2^{31} \approx 2.15 \times 10^9$. (b) $1.37 \times 10^{11}$. (c) 89.5 ms: the floor for any FP32 kernel on this machine.

problems.title: Best-case intensity
problems.statement: Read A and B once, write C once, FP32.
problems.solution: 42.7 and 683 FLOP/byte: far right of any ridge. A large GEMM can always be compute-bound; whether it is depends on reuse.

problems.title: The naive instruction ceiling
problems.statement: The naive kernel's inner loop: two loads, one FMA, one loop branch.

parts.prompt: Fraction of issued instructions that are FMAs, in %?

hints: Even with every load hitting in cache.
problems.solution: 1 in 4 instructions: 25%, so at most 384 GFLOP/s, even before memory is considered. Fast GEMM is about raising that fraction.

problems.title: Naive traffic without caches
problems.statement: Naive GEMM with n = 1024, and suppose every load went to DRAM.

parts.prompt: Time for the FLOPs at peak, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) $8n^3 = 8.6$ GB. (b) 16.8 ms against (c) 1.40 ms: 12× apart. Caches catch much of it in practice, by luck; tiling makes it deliberate.

problems.title: Skinny GEMMs
problems.statement: Best-case intensity with M = N = 4096 and small K (a low-rank update).
problems.solution: (a) 31.0. (b) 3.98: C dominates the traffic ($MN$ elements written), so intensity is about $K/2$. (c) Still above 3, so compute-bound, just. At K = 4 it's below the ridge. Small-K GEMMs are bandwidth problems in disguise.

problems.title: GEMV is GEMM with N = 1

options: Bandwidth: every element of A is used once

hints: A is read once and each element feeds one FMA.
problems.solution: (a) 0.500. (b) Bandwidth. Batching several vectors (N = 8, 16) is how LLM inference makes this compute-bound again: the same A serves more FLOPs.

problems.title: Many tiny GEMMs
problems.statement: 10,000 independent GEMMs of 32 × 32 × 32. A kernel launch costs 5 µs.

parts.prompt: Time at GW-1 peak, in ms?
Launch overhead if each GEMM is its own launch, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) $6.55 \times 10^8$. (b) 0.43 ms. (c) 50 ms: 100× the work. One batched launch (cuBLAS gemmBatched, or a grouped GEMM) is the only sane option.

problems.title: How big for tensor cores?
problems.statement: With tensor cores at 8× FP32, the GW-1's ridge moves to 24 FLOP/byte.

parts.prompt: Smallest n for which square GEMM's best-case intensity exceeds 24?
The intensity a tiled kernel actually achieves is about T/4 for tile size T (Part 2's worked example). Smallest power-of-two T above the ridge?

problems.solution: (a) $n > 144$: n = 145. (b) $T > 96$: T = 128. The problem allows compute-bound execution at modest sizes; the kernel only gets there with tiles of 128, which is why tensor-core GEMMs use 128 × 128 (or bigger) block tiles.

problems.title: Who reads what
problems.statement: Naive kernel for $C = A^\top B$ with all matrices row-major; thread (i, j) computes $C_{ij}$, j from threadIdx.x. At step k a warp reads $A^\top_{ik} = A_{ki}$ and $B_{kj}$.

parts.prompt: The warp's read of A is…
The warp's read of B is…

problems.solution: All lanes share i and k, so A is one address (broadcast). B's 32 lanes read consecutive j: coalesced. Transposes in a GEMM are about which operand is broadcast and which is streamed, which changes the tiling, not the arithmetic.

problems.title: Fused multiply-add

options: two: after the multiply and after the add

parts.prompt: So fma(a, b, c) versus a * b + c with separate instructions…
options: can differ in the last bit, and FMA is usually more accurate

hints: The product is kept exactly before the add.
problems.solution: One rounding, so results can differ from the two-instruction version (compilers contract a*b + c into FMA by default, which is why GPU and CPU results differ in the last bits, Lab 2's tolerance lesson).
